title: Requiem in C minor
hook: Salieri’s “little Requiem, composed by me, and for me”, written for his own funeral and first heard 21 years later.

painting.title: The Cemetery Entrance
painting.collection: Galerie Neue Meister, Staatliche Kunstsammlungen Dresden
painting.pairingNote: Begun around 1825, the year the Requiem was first sung at Salieri’s memorial, it shows a graveyard gate as the threshold between life and death, a fresh grave beyond it, and over the gate the crown of thorns, lance and sponge of Christ’s Passion, the hope of resurrection the Requiem prays for.

facts: Antonio Salieri was the leading musician of the Habsburg court in Vienna: Hofkapellmeister, in charge of the music of the imperial chapel, from 1788 to 1824, longer than anyone before or since. In 1804 he wrote a [[requiem|requiem]], the Catholic Mass for the dead, to be performed at his own funeral. At the head of the score he wrote: “Picciolo Requiem composto da me, e per me, Ant. Salieri, piccolissima creatura” (“A little Requiem, composed by me, and for me, Antonio Salieri, the smallest of creatures”). Why he wrote it then is not known; deaths in his family, the Requiem his teacher Florian Gassmann left unfinished, a new Requiem by Joseph Eybler (1803) and the first printed edition of Mozart’s (1800) may all have played a part.

The work then waited 21 years. Salieri died in Vienna on 7 May 1825, and on 22 June his Requiem was heard for the first time, at the memorial Mass in the Minoritenkirche, the church of Vienna’s Italian community. The court musicians sang and played it under Joseph Eybler, his successor as Hofkapellmeister, the same Eybler who had once begun to complete Mozart’s Requiem.

The music is quiet and devout rather than theatrical, although Salieri was above all an opera composer. The choir carries almost everything, mostly in chords, all voices moving together; the soloists sing only as a group of four. The text is gathered into seven large movements, and the long poem of the Last Judgment, the Dies irae, runs as one continuous movement of about fifteen minutes. The orchestra is the court chapel’s: strings, oboes, bassoons, trumpets, three trombones, timpani and organ, with a [[cor-anglais|cor anglais]] whose plaintive voice opens the work.

Today Salieri is best known through a legend: that he envied Mozart and poisoned him. The rumour began decades after Mozart’s death in 1791, and there is no evidence for it; Mozart’s symptoms do not point to poison. Pushkin’s short play *Mozart and Salieri* (1831), Rimsky-Korsakov’s opera on it (1898) and Peter Shaffer’s *Amadeus* (1979, filmed in 1984) made it famous. The two men were rivals for posts and commissions, but in October 1791 Mozart drove Salieri to *The Magic Flute* and wrote to his wife that there was not a number that did not draw a “Bravo!” from him.
bigPicture.inOneLine: eternal rest and mercy (I), the Day of Judgment in one long movement (II), the Offertory (III), Sanctus and Benedictus (IV–V), Agnus Dei and Communion (VI), and the prayer sung at the coffin (VII).

movements.heading: Introitus and Kyrie
movements.title: Introitus and Kyrie
movements.summary: “Grant them eternal rest, Lord, and let perpetual light shine on them.” The Requiem opens very quietly, with the orchestra alone and a long, sad solo for the cor anglais; then the choir’s basses begin the prayer, and the whole choir answers. The Kyrie (“Lord, have mercy”) follows without a break, a little quicker, and the movement ends slowly again.

mainIdeas.name: The cor anglais
mainIdeas.description: a low, plaintive oboe voice singing long Italian lines over strings.

mainIdeas.name: The plea
mainIdeas.description: soft choral phrases in a gently rocking rhythm, then the full choir at full voice.

notice: Listen to the first minute: no choir, no brass, only a soft orchestra and one reed instrument. Salieri begins his own funeral music as quietly as he can.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Lawrence Foster conducts the Gulbenkian Chorus and Orchestra of Lisbon, recorded live in the Grande Auditório of the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation in November 2009. The Requiem is tracks 1–7 of the album; tracks 8–10 are Beethoven’s *Calm Sea and Prosperous Voyage* and Schubert’s offertory *Intende voci*. Reviewers praised the chorus above all, and the four soloists as a well-matched team.

movements.heading: Sequence: Dies irae
movements.title: Sequence: Dies irae
movements.tempo: Andante maestoso – Allegro molto – Adagio – Andante con moto – Andante maestoso – Larghetto
movements.summary: “Day of wrath, that day will dissolve the world in ashes.” The whole medieval poem of the Last Judgment, set as one continuous movement in six sections at different speeds. Salieri’s Day of Judgment is stately rather than violent: the brass blaze in the “Tuba mirum” and the “Rex tremendae”, but the Confutatis, where Mozart has flames, is calm and resigned. The four soloists sing for the first time here.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: choral cries of “Dies irae!” over strings and bassoons, then trumpets, trombones and timpani.

mainIdeas.name: The Recordare
mainIdeas.description: the soloists as a quartet, taking turns with the choir.

mainIdeas.name: The Lacrimosa
mainIdeas.description: weighty and grand, more a warning than a lament.

stops.hear: A soft, singing passage for the orchestra
stops.happening: The introduction to the Recordare, Andante con moto

stops.hear: The four soloists sing together, always as a group, taking turns with the choir
stops.happening: “Recordare, Jesu pie” (“Remember, kind Jesus”) and the verses of guilt, plea and hope that follow

notice: Salieri sets the whole poem as one movement, almost a quarter of an hour of music. Notice how often the speed changes: each new verse brings a new pace and a new colour.
At the “Confutatis”, about ten and a half minutes in, compare it with Mozart’s: no fire for the damned here, only a quiet acceptance.

movements.heading: Offertory: Domine Jesu and Hostias
movements.title: Offertory: Domine Jesu and Hostias
movements.tempo: Andante maestoso ma con moto – Larghetto
movements.summary: “Lord Jesus Christ, King of glory, free the souls of all the faithful departed from the pains of hell.” The Offertory opens in a stately but moving tempo, turns quick for a choral [[fugue|fugue]] on God’s promise to Abraham, and ends with the calm prayer “Hostias”.

mainIdeas.name: The fugue “Quam olim Abrahae”
mainIdeas.description: voices entering one after another on a lively theme.

stops.hear: Choir and orchestra in a stately, steady tread

stops.hear: Suddenly brisk; the voices enter one after another
stops.happening: “Quam olim Abrahae promisisti” (“as you once promised to Abraham and his seed”), a choral fugue

notice: Listen for the change of pace at about 1:10. The fugue is short, but it is one of the few places where Salieri lets the voices chase each other.

movements.heading: Sanctus
movements.title: Sanctus
movements.tempo: Largo e maestoso – Allegretto non molto
movements.summary: “Holy, holy, holy Lord God of hosts; heaven and earth are full of your glory. Hosanna in the highest.” Slow, solemn calls of “Sanctus”, then a quick, light fugue on “Osanna” that ends on long, firm chords.

mainIdeas.name: The Sanctus
mainIdeas.description: broad, repeated chords, Largo e maestoso.

mainIdeas.name: The Osanna
mainIdeas.description: a nimble fugue, Allegretto non molto.

movements.heading: Benedictus
movements.title: Benedictus
movements.tempo: Andante con moto – Allegretto non molto
movements.summary: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” A gentle, flowing movement in which the four soloists and the choir take turns. It ends with a cheerful “Osanna”, as the Sanctus did.

stops.hear: A gentle, flowing orchestra; the four soloists sing together
stops.happening: “Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini” (“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”), Andante con moto

stops.hear: Quicker and brighter
stops.happening: “Osanna in excelsis”

notice: This is the soloists’ warmest moment. Listen to how they move as one, never one voice against another.

movements.heading: Agnus Dei and Communio
movements.title: Agnus Dei and Communio
movements.summary: “Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, grant them rest.” A forceful, slow opening softens into quiet pleas for rest. The Communion follows, “Let eternal light shine on them, Lord, with your saints for ever”, quicker, with a fugue led by the basses and a final rise in volume on “for you are merciful”.

mainIdeas.name: The fugue “Cum sanctis tuis”
mainIdeas.description: a rolling theme that starts in the basses.

movements.heading: Libera me
movements.title: Libera me
movements.summary: “Deliver me, Lord, from eternal death on that fearful day, when the heavens and the earth shall be moved.” The Libera me is not part of the Mass itself: it is a [[responsory|responsory]] sung beside the coffin after the Requiem, before the burial. Salieri set it as a quiet, simple prayer, with the soloists at its centre, and ends his own funeral music almost abruptly.

stops.hear: The choir, quiet and steady
stops.happening: “Libera me, Domine, de morte aeterna” (“Deliver me, Lord, from eternal death”)

stops.hear: The four soloists, in a simple, song-like tune, answered by the choir
stops.happening: “Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine, et lux perpetua luceat eis”

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Very quiet: the choir almost alone, its lines doubled by a few winds; then the music simply stops
stops.happening: “Quando caeli movendi sunt et terra” (“when the heavens and the earth shall be moved”)

notice: Listen to the very end. There is no grand final chord: the work Salieri wrote for his own funeral closes quietly, almost in mid-thought.

threads.title: For himself
threads.body: “Composed by me, and for me”: Salieri wrote the Requiem as an act of personal devotion and meant it for his own funeral; it waited 21 years to be sung. Its quiet start and its abrupt, quiet end fit that purpose.

threads.title: The choir first
threads.body: The choir sings nearly every word, mostly in [[homophony|homophony]], all voices in the same rhythm so the text is clear. The soloists appear only in the Recordare, the Benedictus and the Libera me, and always as a quartet. Short fugues mark the Offertory, the two Osannas and the Communio.

threads.title: The court orchestra
threads.body: Oboes, bassoons, trumpets, three trombones, timpani, strings and organ, the usual forces of the Viennese court chapel, with the cor anglais added for its sad colour. The brass flare up in the Dies irae; elsewhere the orchestra mostly supports the voices.
